# Study overview {.unlisted}

::: section-card
**Clinical Context & Drug Mechanism**<br> Bictegravir is an integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI) used in combination antiretroviral therapy (cART) to treat HIV-1 and HIV-2. It inhibits HIV integrase, preventing viral DNA integration into the host genome and suppressing viral replication.

**Study Overview: Gajeevy Phase Ia SAD Trial**<br> This report evaluates data from a Phase Ia single ascending dose (SAD) study for **Gajeevy**, a novel investigational drug structurally and mechanistically similar to bictegravir.

**Design:** Four-arm, parallel-group study evaluating single oral doses (10 mg to 100 mg).<br> **Population:** 32 healthy volunteers.<br> **Objectives:** Assess safety and tolerability, explore the maximum tolerated dose (MTD), and perform an initial evaluation of the pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacodynamic (PD) properties of Gajeevy to guide dose selection for Phase II/III trials.<br>
:::

# Main objective {.unlisted}

::: section-card
The overarching objective of this integrative group work is to bridge clinical pharmacology, reproducible data management, and quantitative analysis. Specifically, the project is structured around three core pillars:

**1. Literature Research:** Conduct a comprehensive review of the clinical pharmacology of bictegravir, its mechanism of action as an integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI), and the regulatory and clinical context of Phase I Single Ascending Dose (SAD) studies.<br> **2. FAIR Data Management & Cleaning:** Process, wrangle, and clean the raw dataset strictly adhering to the **FAIR data principles** (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable). This involves maintaining raw data integrity, documenting all data transformation steps transparently, and ensuring reproducible data pipelines in R.<br> **3. Primary Pharmacokinetic (PK) Analysis:** Execute a primary pharmacokinetic analysis on the cleaned dataset to evaluate the pharmacokinetic profile of Gajeevy, including concentration-time profiles and key parameters derived from appropriate quantitative approaches (such as Non-Compartmental Analysis and Compartmental Analysis).
:::

# 1. Bibliographic and contextual work

## 1.1 Literature review

::: section-card
Bictegravir (ATC code: J05AR20) is an integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI) used in HIV treatment. It inhibits HIV integrase, preventing viral DNA integration into the host genome. Combination antiretroviral therapy (cART) can suppress viral replication to undetectable levels, preserve immune function, and prevent disease progression; however, it cannot eradicate HIV from the body.

Bictegravir is marketed in a once-daily fixed-dose combination with emtricitabine and tenofovir alafenamide, both reverse transcriptase inhibitors. It exhibits potent antiviral activity against HIV-1 (EC50 \<0.05–6.6 nM), with a protein-adjusted EC95 of 361 nM (0.162 µg/mL) for wild-type HIV-1, and is also active against HIV-2. A trough concentration of 760 ng/mL (inhibitory quotient = 4.7) was associated with adequate virological suppression in Phase III trials, although no clinically validated exposure target has been established. No upper limit has been defined due to the lack of significant dose-dependent toxicity.

Bictegravir is classified as a Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS) class II drug, characterised by low solubility and high permeability. Its estimated oral bioavailability exceeds 61%, with dose linearity reported between 25 and 100 mg. Peak plasma concentrations are reached within 2–4 hours, and food (moderate‑fat or high‑fat meal) increases AUC by approximately 24% compared to fasted state, without a clinically relevant effect.

Bictegravir exhibits extensive plasma protein binding (\>99%), with an unbound fraction of approximately 0.25% in vitro. It is primarily metabolised by CYP3A and UGT1A1. Approximately 60.5% of a radiolabelled dose is recovered in feces and 35% in urine, predominantly as metabolites; only 1.3% is excreted unchanged in urine. Renal impairment is therefore not expected to substantially affect exposure. Bictegravir is also a substrate of P-glycoprotein (P-gp) and BCRP and has a plasma elimination half-life of approximately 17.3 hours.
:::

## 1.2 Drug development context

::: section-card
The dataset originates from a Phase 1a single ascending dose (SAD) study investigating Gajeevy, an investigational drug with structural and mechanistic similarities to bictegravir. The study was designed as a four-arm, parallel-group study with oral administration.

A total of 32 healthy volunteers received single doses ranging from 10 to 100 mg. The primary objectives were to assess safety and tolerability and, where applicable, explore the maximum tolerated dose. Secondary objectives included characterising the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of Gajeevy. The findings will inform dose selection for subsequent Phase II trials in patients and guide further clinical development. Phase III trials then evaluate the drug’s safety and efficacy in larger patient populations before regulatory approval and market authorisation.
:::

## 1.3 Main pharmacokinetic challenges

- ::: section-card
  Summarize the main pharmacokinetic challenges associated with bictegravir in **no more than five bullet points**.

  - Metabolic drug–drug interactions : Bictegravir is metabolised by both CYP3A and UGT1A1, making its exposure sensitive to enzyme induction or inhibition. For example, rifampicin decreases bictegravir AUC by approximately 75%, potentially compromising antiviral efficacy.

  - Absorption interactions with polyvalent cations : Chelation with magnesium, aluminium, iron or calcium can substantially reduce oral absorption. Simultaneous administration with magnesium/aluminium-containing antacids under fasting conditions decreases bictegravir AUC by approximately 79%, requiring careful administration timing.

  - High plasma protein binding : Bictegravir is highly bound to plasma proteins, limiting its removal by dialysis and complicating the management of excessive exposure or overdose.

  - Pharmacokinetic changes in special populations : Bictegravir exposure is reduced during pregnancy, potentially affecting antiviral coverage. Severe hepatic impairment has not been adequately studied, creating uncertainty regarding exposure and appropriate use in this population.
  :::

## 1.4 Main pharmacodynamic challenges

::: section-card
Summarize the main pharmacodynamic challenges associated with bictegravir in **no more than five bullet points**. Consider mechanism of action, antiviral efficacy, resistance, therapeutic window, and variability in response.

- Dependence on integrase inhibition: Bictegravir inhibits the HIV integrase strand-transfer step, preventing viral DNA integration. Sustained antiviral activity requires sufficient inhibition of this essential replication process.

- Development of viral resistance: Mutations in the HIV integrase gene, including R263K and combinations involving Q148H/K/R, may reduce viral susceptibility to bictegravir and compromise treatment effectiveness.

- Maintaining effective antiviral suppression: Bictegravir has a protein-adjusted EC95 of 361 nM (0.162 µg/mL) against wild-type HIV-1 in vitro. Maintaining adequate antiviral activity is important to minimise virological failure and resistance selection.

- Balancing efficacy and tolerability: Although bictegravir-containing therapy is generally well tolerated, adverse reactions such as headache, diarrhoea and nausea must be considered when evaluating the overall benefit–risk profile.

- Variability in antiviral response: Differences in viral susceptibility, pre-existing resistance mutations and patient-specific factors may influence treatment outcomes, highlighting the importance of virological monitoring and appropriate treatment selection.
:::

# 2. Data handling and management

Data exploration and anomaly screening have been completed. The dataset was examined visually and statistically using `glimpse()`, `summary()`, and distribution plots with `ggplot2` to identify potential outliers, typos, and missing values. All identified irregularities were logged and addressed in our Interim Analysis report.

## 2.1 Dataset Overview and Structure

The dataset was initially explored to understand its structure, identify the available variables, and assess the number of patients and pharmacokinetic observations.

### 2.1.1 Dataset Overview

```{r dataset-overview}
#| echo: false

pa_data |>
  summarise(
    Patients = n_distinct(ID),
    Measured_concentrations = sum(!is.na(`Conc_(ng/mL)`)),
    Analysis_variables = ncol(pa_data) - 2,
    Rows= n(),
    Columns = ncol(pa_data)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Dataset overview")

# One observation per patient for baseline analyses
patient_data <- pa_data |>
  distinct(ID, .keep_all = TRUE)

# Baseline variables: one observation per patient
baseline_vars <- c(
  "BW_(kg)", "AGE", "ALB_(g/L)",
  "CRP_(mg/L)", "CREAT_(mg/dL)"
)
```

## 2.2 Data Preparation and Quality Assessment

Before performing pharmacokinetic analysis, dose variables, missing values, and data consistency were assessed to ensure that the dataset was suitable for subsequent analyses.

### 2.2.1 Dose Variable Preparation

The dose column records administration events. Zero values at subsequent sampling times indicate that no additional dose was administered. These values were recoded as NA for event-based analysis.

A separate patient-level dose variable was created to retain the administered dose across all observations.

```{r dose-handling}
pa_data <- pa_data |>
  arrange(ID, `TIME_(h)`) |>
  group_by(ID) |>
  mutate(
    DOSE_patient = first(`DOSE_(ng)`),
    `DOSE_(ng)` = na_if(`DOSE_(ng)`, 0),
    DOSE_mg = DOSE_patient / 1e6
  ) |>
  ungroup()


```

### 2.2.2 Missing Data Assessment

Missing values were visually assessed to identify their distribution across variables and observations.

Missing concentration values at time zero were distinguished from the dose values recoded as NA at sampling times without additional dosing events. These two types of missing entries have different interpretations and were not treated as equivalent data-quality problems.

```{r missing-visualization}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 9

naniar::vis_miss(pa_data)
```

The missing concentration records occur at time zero, where no baseline concentration measurements were recorded. The NA values in the dose column at subsequent sampling times represent the absence of additional dosing events rather than unknown administered doses.

### 2.2.3 Data Integrity and Consistency Checks

Patient records were assessed for duplicate sampling times, unexpected numbers of records or dosing events, and inconsistent baseline covariates.

```{r integrity-check}

patient_checks <- pa_data |>
  group_by(ID) |>
  summarise(
    Records = n(),
    Unique_times = n_distinct(`TIME_(h)`),
    Dosing_events = sum(`DOSE_(ng)` > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    Covariates_consistent = all(c(
      n_distinct(`BW_(kg)`),
      n_distinct(AGE),
      n_distinct(`ALB_(g/L)`),
      n_distinct(`CRP_(mg/L)`),
      n_distinct(`CREAT_(mg/dL)`),
      n_distinct(SEX),
      n_distinct(ABCG2),
      n_distinct(UGT1A1),
      n_distinct(CYP3A5),
      n_distinct(ABCB1)
    ) == 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

flagged_records <- patient_checks |>
  filter(
    Records != 10 |
    Unique_times != Records |
    Dosing_events != 1 |
    !Covariates_consistent
  )

if (nrow(flagged_records) == 0) {
  cat("No patient-level integrity issues were flagged.")
} else {
  knitr::kable(flagged_records)
}
```

## 2.3 Exploratory Data Analysis and Outlier Screening

Exploratory analyses were performed to examine numerical distributions, identify potentially unusual observations, and investigate relationships among patient characteristics.

### 2.3.1 Univariate Distribution Assessment

The distributions of continuous baseline covariates were examined using one observation per patient to avoid counting repeated measurements multiple times.

Concentration distributions were evaluated using all available concentration measurements to identify potential extreme values.

```{r missing-summary}
# Baseline variables: one observation per patient
baseline_vars <- c(
  "BW_(kg)", "AGE", "ALB_(g/L)",
  "CRP_(mg/L)", "CREAT_(mg/dL)"
)

baseline_long <- patient_data |>
  select(all_of(baseline_vars)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "Value"
  )

# Concentrations: all available observations
conc_long <- pa_data |>
  transmute(
    Variable = "Conc_(ng/mL)",
    Value = `Conc_(ng/mL)`
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(Value))

# Combine and plot
bind_rows(baseline_long, conc_long) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Value)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 12,
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~Variable, scales = "free", ncol = 3) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of numerical variables",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Frequency"
  )
```

### 2.3.2 Concentration–Time Profile Assessment

Some high concentration values were observed during the initial exploration. Since drug concentrations depend on administered dose and sampling time, individual concentration–time profiles were examined separately by dose group to assess their pharmacokinetic plausibility.

```{r concentration-time}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 10

pa_data |>
  filter(!is.na(`Conc_(ng/mL)`)) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = `TIME_(h)`,
    y = `Conc_(ng/mL)`,
    group = ID
  )) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~DOSE_mg,
    labeller = labeller(
      DOSE_mg = function(x) paste(x, "mg")
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Individual concentration-time profiles by dose",
    x = "Time (h)",
    y = "Concentration (ng/mL, log scale)"
  )
```

### 2.3.3 Multivariate Outlier Screening

Potential multivariate outliers were investigated using pairwise scatter plots of patient-level covariates. This approach was used to identify unusual combinations of baseline characteristics that might not be apparent in individual variable distributions.

```{r pairwise-outliers}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-width: 7

patient_data |>
  select(
    AGE,
    `BW_(kg)`,
    `CREAT_(mg/dL)`,
    `ALB_(g/L)`
  ) |>
  GGally::ggpairs()
```

## 2.4 Preparation of the Analysis-Ready Dataset

### 2.4.1 Unit Conversion and Data Export

Following data exploration and quality assessment, the dataset was prepared for subsequent Non-Compartmental Analysis (NCA) and Compartmental Analysis (CA).

To facilitate pharmacokinetic calculations and improve numerical readability, concentration values were converted from ng/mL to µg/mL, and dose values from ng to µg. A repeated-dose variable was also created to associate each subject's administered dose with all corresponding sampling times.

The resulting dataset was intended for use in downstream pharmacokinetic analyses.

```{r}
#| echo: false

library(readr)
library(readxl)
library(dplyr)

# 1. Read the cleaned raw dataset
data_wrong_dose <- read_excel("Data/datIW1PMX006_CLEAN.xlsx")

# 2. Calculate the repeated/maximum dose per subject ID
data_ug <- data_wrong_dose %>%
    group_by(ID) %>%
    mutate(`DOSE_(ng)_repeated` = max(`DOSE_(ng)`)) %>%
    ungroup()

# 3. Convert concentrations from ng/mL to ug/mL
data_ug <- data_ug %>%
  mutate(`Conc_(ng/mL)` = `Conc_(ng/mL)` / 1000) %>%
  rename(`Conc_(ug/mL)` = `Conc_(ng/mL)`)

# 4. Convert doses from ng to ug
data_ug <- data_ug %>%
  mutate(`DOSE_(ng)` = `DOSE_(ng)` / 1000) %>%
  rename(`DOSE_(ug)` = `DOSE_(ng)`)

# 5. Convert repeated doses from ng to ug
data_ug <- data_ug %>%
  mutate(`DOSE_(ng)_repeated` = `DOSE_(ng)_repeated` / 1000) %>%
  rename(`DOSE_(ug)_repeated` = `DOSE_(ng)_repeated`)

# 6. FAIR Principle: Export the processed, analysis-ready dataset securely
#write_csv(data_ug, "Data/datIW1PMX006_UG.csv")
```

## 2.5 Data Management Plan (FAIR)

The Data Management Plan for Gajeevy's Phase Ia SAD study has been developed in accordance with the FAIR principles. The proposed strategy aims to improve data findability through structured documentation, ensure accessibility through controlled access, promote interoperability using standardised data formats and variable definitions, and support reusability through traceable data processing and reproducible pharmacokinetic analyses.

The implementation of these measures will be documented and verified throughout the project, while respecting participant confidentiality and the company's intellectual property requirements.

**The complete Data Management Plan is available here:** [View the complete Data Management Plan](Gajeevy_DMP.pdf.pdf)


# 3. Pharmacokinetic analysis

## 3.1 Non-compartmental analysis (NCA)

### 3.1.1 NCA Methodology

**Aim:** Define and document the analytical settings, integration methods, and acceptance criteria used for the non-compartmental pharmacokinetic analysis (NCA) of Gajeevy.

### NCA Settings & Acceptance Criteria

| Parameter / Setting | Specification | Description / Target |
|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| **Administration Route** | EV | Extravascular administration route |
| **Integration Method** | Linear up / Log down | Trapezoidal rule optimization for ascending/descending phases |
| **Adjusted** $R^2$ | $\ge 0.98$ | Minimum threshold for terminal elimination regression fit |
| **Extrapolated** $\text{AUC}$ | $\le 20\%$ | Maximum allowable percentage of extrapolated area |
| **SPAN Criterion** | $\ge 3$ | Minimum ratio of observation period to estimated half-life in terminal phase |

### Methodology & Workflow

A non-compartmental analysis was performed on our cleaned dataset using `PKAnalix2024R1`. The area under the curve ($\text{AUC}$) was calculated by integrating consecutive segments of the concentration–time curve using the **linear-up/log-down method**. This method more accurately reflects underlying pharmacokinetic behavior and is widely adopted in regulatory guidance and clinical reports.

- **Linear Trapezoidal Rule:** Applied to increasing or constant concentrations, as absorption phases are not straightforwardly described by a single exponent.
- **Log-Linear Trapezoidal Rule:** Applied to decreasing positive concentrations to appropriately capture the exponential decline typical of the elimination phase.

### Quality Control and Reliability Assessment

The reliability of the NCA results was evaluated using three core acceptance criteria: an adjusted $R^2$ of at least $0.98$ for the terminal elimination regression, a maximum extrapolated $\text{AUC}$ fraction of $20\%$, and a SPAN criterion of at least three half-lives within the terminal phase.

- **Regression Evaluation:** The adjusted $R^2$ served as the primary statistical metric, paired with visual inspections of concentration–time plots to confirm a plausible terminal elimination phase.
- **Lambda-z (**$\lambda_z$) Estimation: Five data points were initially selected for the estimation of $\lambda_z$, while aiming to maximize $R^2$.
- **Handling of Deviations:** When acceptance criteria were not met, data points were reassessed and alternative subsets were evaluated based on regression fit and pharmacokinetic plausibility. Estimates failing to meet the criteria were documented and interpreted with appropriate caution.

### Individual Patient Terminal Phase Optimization Log

To ensure optimal estimation of the terminal elimination rate constant ($\lambda_z$), individual concentration–time profiles were evaluated. When standard criteria required deviation from the initial five-point selection, adjustments were documented as follows:

- **Patient 5:** Four data points were selected because the fifth point corresponded to $C_{\text{max}}$, marking the transition between the absorption and elimination phases.
- **Patient 6:** Four data points were selected for the same reason, as the fifth point corresponded to $C_{\text{max}}$ and therefore did not belong to the terminal elimination phase.
- **Patient 7:** Three data points were selected, yielding an adjusted $R^2$ of $0.976$. Although five data points could technically be included, none of the tested subsets met the acceptance criterion of $R^2 \ge 0.98$. The three-point subset provided the highest $R^2$ among the evaluated options while representing the minimum acceptable number of points.
- **Patient 13:** Four data points were selected because the fifth point corresponded to $C_{\text{max}}$, marking the transition between the absorption and elimination phases.
- **Patient 14:** Four data points were selected because including the fifth point resulted in an adjusted $R^2$ below the acceptance criterion of $0.98$.
- **Patient 21:** Four data points were selected because the fifth point corresponded to $C_{\text{max}}$, marking the transition between the absorption and elimination phases.
- **Patient 23:** Four data points were selected because the fifth point corresponded to $C_{\text{max}}$ and did not belong to the terminal elimination phase. The resulting adjusted $R^2$ was $0.973$, remaining slightly below the acceptance criterion of $0.98$.
- **Patient 31:** Four data points were selected because including the fifth point resulted in an adjusted $R^2$ below the acceptance criterion of $0.98$.

## 3.2 Derive and summarize PK parameters

::: section-card
The individual PK parameters were summarized using the mean, standard deviation, median, and interquartile range.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false

nca_data <- read_excel(
  "Data/Data NCA.xlsx")

```

The individual PK parameters were summarized using the mean, standard deviation, median, and interquartile range. The complete individual NCA results are also presented.

```{r nca-parameter-summary111}
#| include: false

pk_parameters <- c(
  "Cmax (ug/mL)",
  "Tmax (h)",
  "AUC0-tlast (h.ug/ml)",
  "AUC0-inf (h.ug/ml)",
  "T1/2 (h)",
  "kel (1/h)",
  "CL/F (mL/h)",
  "Vd/F (mL)"
)

pk_summary <- nca_data |>
  select(all_of(pk_parameters)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "Parameter",
    values_to = "Value"
  ) |>
  group_by(Parameter) |>
  summarise(
    N = sum(!is.na(Value)),
    Mean = round(mean(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    SD = round(sd(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Median = round(median(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Q1 = round(quantile(Value, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Q3 = round(quantile(Value, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Parameter = factor(Parameter, levels = pk_parameters)
  ) |>
  arrange(Parameter)
```

### Pharmacokinetic Parameters Interpretation

The non-compartmental analysis of Gajeevy included 32 healthy volunteers receiving single oral doses of 10, 25, 50 or 100 mg. The results provide an initial understanding of the drug's absorption, exposure, distribution and elimination.

Absorption:The median Tmax is 2.00 h \[1.50–2.00\], indicating that Gajeevy generally reaches its highest plasma concentration approximately two hours after administration. This suggests a relatively early concentration peak, although the extent of oral bioavailability remains unknown.

Systemic exposure:The mean Cmax is 4.09 ± 3.18 µg/mL, while the mean AUC0–inf is 117.18 ± 101.41 h·µg/mL. These values show considerable variability in drug exposure. However, because participants received different doses, part of this variability is expected to result from the study design. Comparing the four dose groups separately would help determine whether exposure increases proportionally with dose.

Elimination:Gajeevy has a mean terminal half-life of 20.12 ± 6.51 h and a mean terminal elimination rate constant of 0.04 ± 0.01 h⁻¹. These findings indicate that plasma concentrations decline relatively slowly during the terminal phase. This could make once-daily administration worth investigating, but repeated-dose studies are needed to confirm whether effective concentrations can be maintained over 24 hours.

Clearance and distribution:The mean apparent oral clearance is 436.38 ± 109.48 mL/h, and the mean apparent volume of distribution is 11.89 ± 2.52 L. Since absolute oral bioavailability is unknown, these parameters cannot be interpreted as the true clearance or volume of distribution of Gajeevy.

Reliability of exposure estimates:The mean AUC0–inf (117.18 h·µg/mL) is higher than the mean AUC0–tlast (92.16 h·µg/mL). This difference indicates that part of the total exposure was estimated beyond the last measured concentration. The reliability of this estimation should be checked using individual extrapolated AUC percentages.

### Comparison of Gajeevy and Bictegravir PK parameters\*\*

1.  **50mg dose group**

***Quantitative comparison: 50mg group Gajeevy Vs RCP***

|             |                            |              |
|-------------|----------------------------|--------------|
| Parameters  | Observed values for 50mg   | RCP          |
| T1/2        | 17,96h                     | 17,3h        |
| Tmax        | 2,00h                      | 2,0 - 4h     |
| Cmax        | 4,73µg/mL                  | 6.15 µg/mL   |
| AUC 0-inf   | 110.56 µg·h/mL             | 102 µg·h/mL  |

Test 1; Relation between Kel and T1/2

T1/2= ln2/ Kel

```         
    = ln2/ 0,04 = 17,3h 
```

This matches exactly with the T1/2 of the RCP (17,3h). So, the Kel derived perfectly reproduces the official half-life of bictegravir

Test 2: Relation between CL/F= dose/AUC

CL/F= 50000µg/110,56

```         
     = 452,24 ml/h 
```

From the RCP, for the 50000µg dose and AUC of 102µg.h/ml, we have a CL/F of 490,2ml/h.

This still falls within the confidence for gajeevy (335.10 - 516.94). So, this is also a solid validation for our derived parameters.

***Dose-Proportionality (Linearity) Assessment***

Dose-Normalized AUC Calculation (from the table)

The multiple dose pharmacokinetics of bictegravir are dose proportional over the dose range of 25 to 100 mg. Dose proportionality helps predict drug exposure when the dose changes and is consistent with linear pharmacokinetics over the studied dose range. We can assess dose proportionality by comparing dose-normalized AUC values (AUC/dose) across groups.

|           |               |                       |
|-----------|---------------|-----------------------|
| **Dose**  | **AUC0-inf**  | **AUC/Dose (ratio)**  |
| 10 mg     | 24.35         | 2.44                  |
| 25 mg     | 57.34         | 2.29                  |
| 50 mg     | 110.56        | 2.21                  |
| 100 mg    | 264.12        | 2.64                  |

Interpretation : The ratios remain within a relatively stable range (2,2 – 2,6). This is consistent with the RCP statement (dose-proportional linearity between 25 and 100mg)

\*\*\*Vd/F for the 50mg group The Vd/F for gajeevy is 10727,32 L which falls within the reference range (10,900-11,200 mL). This support the structural validity of our derived parameter.

References:

-Ekobena, Pierre, Myriam Briki, Kim Dao, et al. « Population Pharmacokinetics of Bictegravir in Real-World People with HIV ». The Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy 80, no 10 (2025).

-European Medicines Agency (EMA). Biktarvy: Summary of Product Characteristics. Annex I, Section 5.2 – Pharmacokinetic Properties.

2.  **Group of 10,25 and 100mg doses Parameters to parameters comparison**

***Half-life (t½, hours)***

|                |                   |                     |
|----------------|-------------------|---------------------|
| **Dose**       | **Derived t1/2**  | **Gallant Day 10**  |
| 10 mg vs 5 mg  | 21.37             | 20.8                |
| 25 mg          | 16.99             | 15.9                |
| 100 mg         | 20.12             | 20.9                |

Interpretation: Near-perfect agreement across all dose levels. This strongly validates our derived parameters — t½ is dose-independent, exactly as expected for a drug with linear PK.

***Tmax (hours)***

|                |                   |                     |
|----------------|-------------------|---------------------|
| **Dose**       | **Derived Tmax**  | **Gallant Day 10**  |
| 10 mg vs 5 mg  | 2,0               | 1,5                 |
| 25 mg          | 1,75              | 1,3                 |
| 50 mg          | 2,0               | 1,8                 |
| 100 mg         | 2,0               | 2,7                 |

Interpretation: Overlapping ranges, consistent with rapid oral absorption (1-3h) typical of bictegravir. Minor differences fall well within biological/inter-individual variability.

***AUC (µg·h/mL) — direct comparison***

|                |                         |                              |
|----------------|-------------------------|------------------------------|
| **Dose**       | **Derived AUC0-tlast**  | **Gallant AUCtau (Day 10)**  |
| 10 mg vs 5 mg  | 18.09                   | 9.98                         |
| 25 mg          | 45.16                   | 48.95                        |
| 100 mg         | 200.62                  | 178.90                       |

Interpretation: Remarkably close (within \~15%) given that we are comparing single-dose exposure to steady-state exposure. This is a good sign — bictegravir accumulates modestly (AR_AUC \~1.25-1.9x per Gallant), so our single-dose AUC should be lower than Day 10 AUC for the patient with 10mg dose.

***Cmax (µg/mL)***

Direct comparison (Our single-dose vs. Gallant Day 10 steady-state):

|           |                              |                                   |
|-----------|------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| **Dose**  | **derived Cmax** **Gajeevy** | **Gallant Cmax(µg/ml) (Day 10)**  |
| 25 mg     | 2.08                         | 3.475                             |
| 100 mg    | 8.84                         | 12.235                            |

At first glance this looks like a meaningful underestimation. But Gallant’s Day 10 Cmax already includes accumulation (AR_Cmax). If we back-calculate the Day 1 (single-dose) Cmax using their reported accumulation ratios:

|           |                                      |                       |
|-----------|--------------------------------------|-----------------------|
| **Dose**  | **Gallant Day 1 (back-calculated)**  | **Our derived Cmax**  |
| 25 mg     | 3,475/1.385 = 2.51                   | 2.08                  |
| 50 mg     | 6,080/1.220 = 4.98                   | 4.73                  |
| 100 mg    | 12,235/1.684 = 7.27                  | 8.84                  |

Interpretation: Once corrected for accumulation, our Cmax values align very well with the literature’s single-dose Cmax. This strongly supports the parameters we derived from our dataset.

***CL/F (mL/h)***

|                |                   |                     |
|----------------|-------------------|---------------------|
| **Dose**       | **Derived CL/F**  | **Gallant CLss/F**  |
| 10 mg vs 5 mg  | 410.96            | 523.8               |
| 25 mg          | 446.67            | 567.3               |
| 50 mg          | 457.79            | 621.9               |
| 100 mg         | 379.51            | 570.6               |

Interpretation: The clearance estimates are consistently 20-35% lower than steady-state literature values. This is internally consistent with slightly higher AUC we obtained (lower CL/F → higher exposure for same dose, since CL/F = Dose/AUC).

***Vd/F (mL)***

|                |                   |                   |
|----------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| **Dose**       | **Derived Vd/F**  | **Gallant Vz/F**  |
| 10 mg vs 5 mg  | 14,051            | 15,527            |
| 25 mg          | 11,353            | 13,232            |
| 50 mg          | 10,727            | 15,559            |
| 100 mg         | 11,166            | 17,621            |

Interpretation: Same order of magnitude throughout (10-18 L). Our values run systematically 10-35% lower, but this is a minor and plausible discrepancy.

*Reference: Gallant, Joel E., Melanie Thompson, Edwin DeJesus, et al. « Antiviral Activity, Safety, and Pharmacokinetics of Bictegravir as 10-Day Monotherapy in HIV-1-Infected Adults ». Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes (1999) 75, no 1 (2017).*

## 3.3 Covariate analysis

::: section-card
To investigate potential relationships between pharmacokinetic parameters and patient characteristics, Spearman's rank correlation analysis was performed. Five continuous covariates were evaluated: age, body weight, albumin, CRP, and creatinine.

The Spearman correlation coefficient (ρ) and its corresponding p-value were calculated for each relationship. These analyses were considered exploratory.
:::

```{r prepare-pk-covariates}
#| include: false

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

# Prepare data for covariate analysis
nca_cov <- nca_data |>
  mutate(
    Dose_mg = DOSE_ug_repeated / 1000,
    Dose_group = factor(Dose_mg),

    Cmax_per_mg = `Cmax (ug/mL)` / Dose_mg,
    AUC_last_per_mg = `AUC0-tlast (h.ug/ml)` / Dose_mg,
    AUC_inf_per_mg = `AUC0-inf (h.ug/ml)` / Dose_mg
  )

# Continuous covariates
continuous_covars <- c(
  "AGE",
  "BW_kg_",
  "ALB_g_L_",
  "CREAT_mg_dL_",
  "CRP_mg_L_"
)

# PK parameters
pk_parameters <- c(
  "Cmax (ug/mL)",
  "Tmax (h)",
  "AUC0-inf (h.ug/ml)",
  "T1/2 (h)",
  "kel (1/h)",
  "CL/F (mL/h)",
  "Vd/F (mL)"
)

# Readable covariate names for plots
cov_labels <- c(
  "Age (years)",
  "Body weight (kg)",
  "Albumin (g/L)",
  "Creatinine (mg/dL)",
  "CRP (mg/L)"
)
```

```{r pk-covariate-correlations.}
#| include: false

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(knitr)

# PK parameters
pk_parameters <- c(
  "Cmax (ug/mL)",
  "Tmax (h)",
  "AUC0-inf (h.ug/ml)",
  "T1/2 (h)",
  "kel (1/h)",
  "CL/F (mL/h)",
  "Vd/F (mL)"
)

# Continuous covariates
continuous_covars <- c(
  "AGE",
  "BW_kg_",
  "ALB_g_L_",
  "CREAT_mg_dL_",
  "CRP_mg_L_"
)

# Covariate labels
cov_labels <- c(
  "Age (years)",
  "Body weight (kg)",
  "Albumin (g/L)",
  "Creatinine (mg/dL)",
  "CRP (mg/L)"
)

# Reshape data
corr_long <- nca_cov |>
  select(
    id, Dose_group,
    all_of(continuous_covars),
    all_of(pk_parameters)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(continuous_covars),
    names_to = "Covariate",
    values_to = "X"
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(pk_parameters),
    names_to = "PK_parameter",
    values_to = "Y"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Covariate = factor(
      Covariate,
      levels = continuous_covars,
      labels = cov_labels
    )
  )

# Calculate Spearman correlations
cor_results <- corr_long |>
  group_by(PK_parameter, Covariate) |>
  group_modify(~{
    d <- .x |>
      filter(is.finite(X), is.finite(Y))

    if (
      nrow(d) < 4 ||
      n_distinct(d$X) < 2 ||
      n_distinct(d$Y) < 2
    ) {
      return(tibble(
        N = nrow(d),
        rho = NA_real_,
        p_value = NA_real_
      ))
    }

    test <- suppressWarnings(
      cor.test(
        d$X, d$Y,
        method = "spearman",
        exact = FALSE
      )
    )

    tibble(
      N = nrow(d),
      rho = unname(test$estimate),
      p_value = test$p.value
    )
  }) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    Plot_label = paste0(
      "rho = ", sprintf("%.2f", rho),
      "\np = ", format.pval(p_value, digits = 2)
    )
  )

# Function to display results for each PK parameter
show_cor <- function(parameter) {

  cor_results |>
    filter(PK_parameter == parameter) |>
    select(Covariate, N, rho, p_value) |>
    mutate(
      rho = round(rho, 2),
      p_value = format.pval(p_value, digits = 3)
    ) |>
    knitr::kable(
      caption = paste("Spearman correlation:", parameter)
    , align = "cccc")
}
```

::: section-card
Spearman's rho (ρ) describes the strength and direction of the association between two variables, ranging from −1 to +1. Positive values indicate a positive association, whereas negative values indicate an inverse association. The p-value is used to assess statistical evidence against the null hypothesis of no association.

The results should be interpreted cautiously because the analysis is exploratory and includes patients receiving different dose levels.
:::

### 3.3.2 PK parameter–covariate relationships

Scatterplots were used to visualize the relationships between individual PK parameters and continuous patient covariates. Patients were colored according to their administered dose. Spearman's correlation coefficient (ρ) and the corresponding p-value are displayed for each relationship.

```{r prepare-correlation-plots}
#| include: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# Function to plot each PK parameter
plot_pk_cov <- function(parameter) {

  plot_data <- corr_long |>
    filter(
      PK_parameter == parameter,
      is.finite(X),
      is.finite(Y)
    )

  plot_stats <- cor_results |>
    filter(PK_parameter == parameter)

  ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = X, y = Y)) +
    geom_point(
      aes(color = Dose_group),
      size = 2.3,
      alpha = 0.85
    ) +
    geom_smooth(
      method = "lm",
      formula = y ~ x,
      se = FALSE,
      color = "black",
      linetype = "dashed",
      linewidth = 0.6
    ) +
    geom_label(
      data = plot_stats,
      aes(
        x = -Inf,
        y = Inf,
        label = Plot_label
      ),
      inherit.aes = FALSE,
      hjust = 0,
      vjust = 1,
      size = 3,
      fill = "white",
      label.size = 0
    ) +
    facet_wrap(
      ~Covariate,
      scales = "free_x",
      ncol = 3
    ) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
      legend.position = "bottom"
    ) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Covariate relationships:", parameter),
      x = NULL,
      y = parameter,
      color = "Dose (mg)"
    )
}
```

## 3.4 Compartmental modelling

### 3.4.1 CA Methodology

**Aim**: Develop a preliminary compartmental model to describe the pharmacokinetics of Gajeevy following single-dose oral administration and compare alternative model structures.

A compartmental analysis (CA) was performed on our clean dataset in PKAnalix2024R1.

NCA provided an initial overview of the pharmacokinetic characteristics of Gajeevy following oral administration, without assuming a specific compartmental model. The observed concentration-time profiles of Gajeevy (@fig-Gajeevy-concentration-time-profiles), together with the NCA-derived parameters, were subsequently used to guide the selection of a preliminary compartmental model.

Model selection was based on the goodness of fit and information criteria, taking into account the trade-off between model complexity and descriptive performance.

```{r}
#| label: fig-Gajeevy-concentration-time-profiles
#| eval: true
#| fig-cap: "Concentration-time profiles following the oral administration of Gajeevy on both linear and log scale."

#load necessary packages
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

#load data
data_CA <- data_file
# Plot 1: Linear scale
p1 <- ggplot(data_CA, aes(
  x = TIME_.h.,
  y = Conc_.ug.mL.,
  group = ID
)) +
  geom_line(
    color = "#0072B2",
    alpha = 0.45,
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  stat_summary(
    aes(group = 1),
    fun = mean,
    geom = "line",
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 50, by = 10),
    limits = c(0, 50),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 10, by = 2.5),
    limits = c(0, 10),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Linear scale",
    x = "Time (h)",
    y = expression(Concentration~(mu*g/mL))
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, hjust = 0.5),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
    panel.grid.minor = element_line(color = "#EEEEEE"),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#D9D9D9")
  )

# Plot 2: Logarithmic scale
p2 <- ggplot(data_CA, aes(
  x = TIME_.h.,
  y = Conc_.ug.mL.,
  group = ID
)) +
  geom_line(
    color = "#0072B2",
    alpha = 0.45,
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  stat_summary(
    aes(group = 1),
    fun = mean,
    geom = "line",
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 50, by = 10),
    limits = c(0, 50),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))
  ) +
  scale_y_log10(
    breaks = c(0.1, 1, 10),
    limits = c(0.05, 15),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Log scale",
    x = "Time (h)",
    y = expression(Concentration~(mu*g/mL))
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, hjust = 0.5),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
    panel.grid.minor = element_line(color = "#EEEEEE"),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#D9D9D9")
  )

# Combine both plots
combined_plot <- (p1 | p2)
combined_plot
```

### 3.4.2 Compartment selection and evaluation

### Initial model selection

NCA provided an initial overview of the pharmacokinetic characteristics of Gajeevy following oral administration, without assuming a specific compartmental model. The observed concentration–time profiles (@fig-Gajeevy-concentration-time-profiles), together with the NCA-derived parameters, were subsequently used to guide the selection of a preliminary compartmental model. The concentration–time profile supports the selection of an oral one-compartment model with first-order absorption and elimination. A characteristic oral absorption pattern is observed, with concentrations increasing exponentially from the first sampling point at 0.5 hours to a peak concentration at approximately 2 hours, followed by a gradual decline. This resembles a linear absorption process from the gastrointestinal tract into the systemic circulation, as no clear plateau is observed before (T\_{\max}), and (C\_{\max}). Subsequently AUC appears to increase approximately proportionally with dose, as shown in Figure 1.2. and table of NCA. These observations suggest dose-proportional pharmacokinetics and support the use of a one-compartment model with first-order absorption. As no data were available before the first sampling point, no absorption lag time was included, keeping the model as simple as possible without introducing an additional parameter unsupported by the available data. The post-peak decline appears approximately linear on the semi-logarithmic scale from 2 to 48 hours, which is consistent with first-order elimination. Finally, the absence of an obvious inflection point indicating a distinct distribution phase supports the use of a one-compartment model as a reasonable starting point.

### Comparing a two-compartment system

However, when we look at the concentration-time curves per dose (@fig-Gajeevy-concentration-time-profiles-per_dose), we see a slight bend (inflection point) between 4 and 8 hours after dosing in all dose groups. This could indicate a two-compartment system, in which the drug distributes into a second compartment. When we fit this model to our data, the two-compartment model yields a lower -2LL (-532.8 versus -442.7), and thus a better raw fit to the data (@tbl-ca-model-comparison). This is consistent with the fact that models with more parameters can always follow the data at least as closely, so -2LL rewards additional parameters, even when these mainly capture noise. Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), however, also correct for model complexity by penalizing each additional parameter (AIC = -2LL + 2 × number of parameters; BIC = -2LL + ln(n) × number of parameters), so that a model only wins if it improves the fit by more than the penalty costs. Because each individual was fitted separately, the two-compartment model has 64 more parameters than the one-compartment model (161 versus 97), and this additional complexity is not justified by the gain in fit: both the AIC (-248.7 versus -210.8) and the BIC (-226.1 versus -175.6) are lower for the one-compartment model (@tbl-ca-model-comparison). The slight bend observed between 4 and 8 hours may reflect variability or noise in the data rather than a true distribution phase. The two-compartment model, being more flexible, can follow this deviation, but the data do not support a distinct second compartment.

```{r}
#| label: fig-Gajeevy-concentration-time-profiles-per_dose
#| eval: true
#| fig-cap: "Concentration-time profiles separated on dose following the oral administration of Gajeevy on log scale."

dose_plot <- ggplot(data_CA, aes(x = TIME_.h., y = Conc_.ug.mL., group = ID, color = factor(DOSE_.ug._repeated))) +
  geom_line(
    aes(group = ID),
    alpha = 0.40,
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  stat_summary(
    aes(group = factor(DOSE_.ug._repeated)),
    fun = mean,
    geom = "line",
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1", name = "Dose (µg)") +
  theme_light() +
  labs(
    title = "Concentration-time profiles by dose on log scale",
    x = "Time (h)",
    y = "Concentration (µg/L, log scale)"
  )
dose_plot
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ca-model-comparison
#| eval: true
#| tbl-cap: "Fit criteria for one- and two-compartment models"

model_comparison <- data.frame(
  Criterion = c(
    "Total cost",
    "-2 Log-likelihood (-2LL)",
    "Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)",
    "Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC)",
    "Number of estimated parameters"
  ),
  `One-compartment model` = c(
    1.16, -442.72, -248.72, -226.13, 97
  ),
  `Two-compartment model` = c(
    0.85, -532.77, -210.77, -175.55, 161
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  model_comparison,
  digits = 2)
```

The preliminary one-compartment model is therefore the simpler and more reliable choice, and it describes the data adequately. This was further supported by the observed-versus-predicted plot (@fig-observed-versus-predicted-plot), which showed no clear curvature or trend indicating systematic over- or underestimation of concentrations. A sketch of the model structure is shown in @fig-sketch-model.
